cases.title: Bat echolocation call and its single most similar labeled call
cases.context: In a study of bat echolocation (the use of echoes from emitted calls to locate objects), the duration and the peak frequency (the frequency that carries the most energy) of recorded calls were measured. Both measures were rescaled to a 0 to 10 scale, so the scaled values are unitless. Four recorded calls had already been labeled by call type from video of the flight path. A new unlabeled call had a scaled duration of 6 and a scaled peak frequency of 4.
tasks: Calculate the Euclidean distance from the new call (6, 4) to each of the four labeled calls. Make sure to show your intermediate calculations.
Assign the new call to the call type of the single labeled call it is most similar to. State whether this is a clustering or a classification problem. Please state how you reached your conclusions.

steps.title: Identify the problem type
steps.words: The four recorded calls have known call types, so assigning the new call is a classification problem (supervised).

steps.title: Distance to call 1 and call 2
steps.words: Subtract matching features, square, add and take the root.

steps.title: Distance to call 3 and call 4
steps.words: The same formula is applied to every labeled call.

steps.title: Pick the most similar call
steps.words: Call 2 has the smallest distance, so it is the most similar call. Its call type is Search call, so the new call is assigned to Search call.

cases.conclusion: The nearest labeled call is call 2 at distance 2.23607, so the new call is classified as a search call. This is a classification problem because the call types of the recorded calls are known. It uses only one neighbor (K = 1).

cases.title: Three distances between two personality score profiles
cases.context: In a study of personality, university students completed a questionnaire that gives an extraversion score (how outgoing and sociable a person is) and a neuroticism score (how strongly a person tends to feel worry and negative mood). Each score ranges from 0 to 48 points. The table below shows the scores of two of the students. The researchers wanted to know how dissimilar the two score profiles were before clustering the whole sample.
tasks: Calculate the Euclidean distance and the Manhattan distance between student A and student B. Make sure to show your intermediate calculations.
Calculate the Minkowski distance with p = 3 between the two students and compare all three values.
cases.symbols: \(q,r\) (two points or feature vectors), \(q_i,r_i\) (their \(i\)th coordinates), \(m\) (number of dimensions), \(p\) (Minkowski order), \(d(q,r)\) (distance).

steps.title: Coordinate differences
steps.words: Find the absolute difference for each feature first, then reuse them in every formula.

steps.title: Euclidean distance
steps.words: Square, add and take the square root.

steps.title: Manhattan distance
steps.words: Add the absolute differences.

steps.title: Minkowski distance, p = 3
steps.words: Cube, add and take the cube root.

steps.title: Compare
steps.words: Larger p puts more weight on the largest single difference, so the distance shrinks toward the largest difference, 14. All three distances describe the same pair of students.

cases.conclusion: The Euclidean distance between student A and student B is 16.64332, the Manhattan distance is 23, and the Minkowski distance with p = 3 is 15.1438.

cases.title: Three distances between two symptom profiles
cases.context: In a clinical study of mood and anxiety, patients rated their symptoms on two questionnaires. One questionnaire gives an anxiety score (frequency of worry and tension over the past two weeks) and the other gives a low mood score (frequency of sadness and loss of interest over the past two weeks). Each score ranges from 0 to 21 points. The table below shows the scores of two patients who were seen on the same day.
tasks: Calculate the Euclidean distance and the Manhattan distance between the symptom profiles of patient 1 and patient 2. Make sure to show your intermediate calculations.
Calculate the Minkowski distance with p = 3 between the two symptom profiles and compare all three values.
cases.symbols: \(q,r\) (two points or feature vectors), \(q_i,r_i\) (their \(i\)th coordinates), \(m\) (number of dimensions), \(p\) (Minkowski order), \(d(q,r)\) (distance).

steps.title: Coordinate differences
steps.words: Find the absolute difference for each feature first, then reuse them in every formula.

steps.title: Euclidean distance
steps.words: Square, add and take the square root.

steps.title: Manhattan distance
steps.words: Add the absolute differences.

steps.title: Minkowski distance, p = 3
steps.words: Cube, add and take the cube root.

steps.title: Compare
steps.words: Larger p puts more weight on the largest single difference, so the distance shrinks toward the largest difference, 11. Patient 1 scores higher on anxiety and patient 2 scores higher on low mood, and the absolute values remove the signs.

cases.conclusion: The Euclidean distance between patient 1 and patient 2 is 12.52996, the Manhattan distance is 17, and the Minkowski distance with p = 3 is 11.56547.

cases.title: k-means on nine bedtimes (sleep chronotypes)
cases.context: In a study of sleep chronotypes (a person's natural tendency to sleep early or late), 9 university students wore a wrist activity monitor for two weeks. The average bedtime of each student was recorded in minutes (min) after 9 pm. The average bedtimes were 15, 30, 40, 85, 120, 150, 165, 180 and 195 min. The researchers wanted to group the students by bedtime with the k-Means algorithm, using k = 2 and the initial centroids c1 = 30 and c2 = 100.
tasks: Perform iteration 1 of the k-Means algorithm. Calculate both distances for every bedtime, assign the cluster labels and calculate the new centroids. Make sure to show your intermediate calculations.
Continue iterating until no cluster label changes. Provide the final cluster labels and the final centroids.
cases.symbols: \(x_i\) (feature vector of entry \(i\)), \(c_j\) (centroid of cluster \(j\)), \(d_{ij}\) (distance from entry \(i\) to centroid \(j\)), \(y_i\) (cluster label of entry \(i\)), \(n_j\) (number of entries in cluster \(j\)), \(k\) (number of clusters).

steps.title: Set up
steps.words: In one dimension the Euclidean distance is the absolute difference.

steps.title: Iteration 1 distances
steps.words: Every bedtime gets a distance to both centroids. The full table lists all nine rows.

steps.title: Iteration 1 labels
steps.words: Bedtimes 15, 30 and 40 are closer to 30. Bedtimes of 85 and above are closer to 100.

steps.title: Iteration 1 centroids
steps.words: Each centroid is the mean of its members.

steps.title: Iteration 2 distances and labels
steps.words: Bedtime 85 is now closer to the first centroid, so it moves to cluster 1. A label changed, so the algorithm continues.

steps.title: Iteration 2 centroids
steps.words: Recompute both means with the new memberships.

steps.title: Iteration 3 check
steps.words: No label changes, so the centroids stay the same and the algorithm stops.

steps.title: Name the clusters
steps.words: The labels 1 and 2 can be named early chronotype and late chronotype after clustering.

cases.conclusion: Iteration 1 moves the centroids from 30 and 100 to 28.33333 and 149.16667. Iteration 2 moves bedtime 85 into cluster 1 and gives 42.5 and 162. Iteration 3 changes nothing, so the final clusters are bedtimes 15 to 85 min (early) and 120 to 195 min (late).

cases.title: Single k-means iteration: mice in an open field
cases.context: In a study of exploratory behaviour, 4 mice were each placed in an open field arena (a large empty box that is filmed from above) for 10 minutes. The time spent in the centre of the arena (Centre time, in seconds, s) and the total distance travelled (Distance, in metres, m) were measured for each mouse. The data were standardized to avoid any issues associated with differences in scale; the scaled data are unitless.
tasks: Based on the resulting data listed in the table below, perform a single iteration of the k-Means algorithm with k = 2. Use the Euclidian distance formula for your calculations. Use the following two initial centroids: C1 (Centre time = 1, Distance = 1) and C2 (Centre time = 5, Distance = 5).

As part of your final answer, provide the cluster labels for each of the 4 data points AND the new centroids of the two updated clusters after this single iteration. Make sure to show your intermediate calculations.
cases.symbols: \(x_i\) (feature vector of entry \(i\)), \(c_j\) (centroid of cluster \(j\)), \(d_{ij}\) (distance from entry \(i\) to centroid \(j\)), \(y_i\) (cluster label of entry \(i\)), \(n_j\) (number of entries in cluster \(j\)), \(k\) (number of clusters).

steps.title: Distances for mouse 1
steps.words: Mouse 1 is (1, 2).

steps.title: Distances for mouse 2
steps.words: Mouse 2 is (3, 2).

steps.title: Distances for mouse 3
steps.words: Mouse 3 is (6, 5).

steps.title: Distances for mouse 4
steps.words: Mouse 4 is (7, 8).

steps.title: Assign labels
steps.words: Each mouse goes to the centroid with the smaller distance.

steps.title: New centroids
steps.words: Cluster 1 averages mice 1 and 2. Cluster 2 averages mice 3 and 4. Each feature is averaged separately.

cases.title: Single k-means iteration: EEG power during a breathing exercise
cases.context: In a study of meditation, electroencephalography (EEG, a recording of the brain's electrical activity from the scalp) was used to measure alpha power (Alpha, the strength of the 8 to 12 Hz brain rhythm, in μV²) and theta power (Theta, the strength of the 4 to 8 Hz brain rhythm, in μV²) in 5 adults during a slow breathing exercise. tasks: Based on the resulting data listed in the table below, perform a single iteration of the k-Means algorithm with k = 2. Use the Euclidian distance formula for your calculations. Use the following two initial centroids: C1 (Alpha = 3, Theta = 3) and C2 (Alpha = 6, Theta = 6).

As part of your final answer, provide the cluster labels for each of the 5 data points AND the new centroids of the two updated clusters after this single iteration. Make sure to show your intermediate calculations.

steps.title: Distances for subject 1
steps.words: Subject 1 is (2, 6).

steps.title: Distances for subject 2

cases.title: Within-cluster sums of squares for ten hearing thresholds
cases.context: In a study of hearing in older adults, the pure-tone hearing threshold (the quietest 4 kHz tone that a listener can detect) was measured in decibels hearing level (dB HL) in 10 listeners. The thresholds were 6, 9, 12, 15, 21, 48, 52, 57, 63 and 68 dB HL. The thresholds were clustered in R with kmeans(threshold, c(10, 40)). The final clusters were 6, 9, 12, 15, 21 (centroid 12.6) and 48, 52, 57, 63, 68 (centroid 57.6). The table below shows the size (number of points in each cluster), withinss (within-cluster sum of squares) and tot.withinss (total within-cluster sum of squares) fields that R returned for k = 1 to 4.
tasks: Calculate the within-cluster sum of squares (SS) for each of the two clusters and tot.withinss for k = 2. Calculate betweenss (between-cluster sum of squares) from the total sum of squares. Make sure to show your intermediate calculations.
Using tot.withinss for k = 1 to 4, how many clusters should be used? Please state how you reached your conclusions.
cases.symbols: \(SS_j\) (within-cluster sum of squares of cluster \(j\)), \(x_i\) (entry value), \(c_j\) (centroid of cluster \(j\)), \(y_i\) (cluster label), \(k\) (number of clusters).

steps.title: Cluster 1 sum of squares
steps.words: Square each deviation from the cluster 1 centroid and add.

steps.title: Cluster 2 sum of squares
steps.words: Square each deviation from the cluster 2 centroid and add.

steps.title: Total within-cluster sum of squares
steps.words: This is tot.withinss in the R output.

steps.title: Between-cluster sum of squares
steps.words: R reports this as betweenss, 5062.5. At k = 1 the whole total is within-cluster.

steps.title: Compare k = 1 to 4
steps.words: The drop from k = 1 to k = 2 is about 5062.5. The later drops are about 208 and 97.2.

steps.title: Choose k
steps.words: Beyond k = 2 there is only modest improvement, so two clusters of listeners are chosen. They can be named better hearing and poorer hearing.

cases.conclusion: withinss is 133.2 and 261.2, tot.withinss is 394.4, and betweenss is 5062.5. tot.withinss improves only modestly for k > 2, so k = 2 is chosen.

cases.title: Within-cluster sums of squares for ten cortisol samples
cases.context: In a study of stress, saliva was collected from 10 students 30 minutes after waking, and the cortisol concentration (cortisol is a hormone released in response to stress) was measured in nanomoles per litre (nmol/L). The concentrations were 5, 6, 8, 14, 15, 17, 18, 27, 29 and 31 nmol/L. The concentrations were clustered in R with kmeans(cortisol, c(8, 29)). The final clusters were 5, 6, 8, 14, 15, 17, 18 (centroid 11.85714) and 27, 29, 31 (centroid 29). The table below shows the size (number of points in each cluster), withinss (within-cluster sum of squares) and tot.withinss (total within-cluster sum of squares) fields that R returned for k = 1 to 4.
tasks: Calculate the within-cluster sum of squares (SS) for each of the two clusters and tot.withinss for k = 2. Calculate betweenss (between-cluster sum of squares) from the total sum of squares. Make sure to show your intermediate calculations.
Using tot.withinss for k = 1 to 4, how many clusters should be used? Please state how you reached your conclusions.
cases.symbols: \(SS_j\) (within-cluster sum of squares of cluster \(j\)), \(x_i\) (entry value), \(c_j\) (centroid of cluster \(j\)), \(y_i\) (cluster label), \(k\) (number of clusters).

steps.title: Cluster 1 sum of squares
steps.words: Use the unrounded centroid 83/7 to avoid rounding drift. Square each deviation from it and add.

steps.title: Cluster 2 sum of squares
steps.words: Square each deviation from the cluster 2 centroid and add.

steps.title: Total within-cluster sum of squares
steps.words: This is tot.withinss in the R output.

steps.words: R reports this as betweenss, 617.1429. At k = 1 the whole total is within-cluster.

cases.title: Classifying a songbird call with K = 3
cases.context: In a study of songbird communication, the duration (in milliseconds, ms) and the peak frequency (the frequency that carries the most energy, in kilohertz, kHz) of 5 recorded calls were measured. Each call was labeled as an Alarm call or a Contact call from the behaviour of the flock when the call was given. The data were standardized to avoid any issues associated with differences in scale; the scaled data are unitless. A new call was then recorded with a scaled duration of 5 and a scaled peak frequency of 5. The 5 labeled calls were measured with the following results (training set):
tasks: Calculate the Euclidean distance from the new call (5, 5) to each of the 5 labeled calls, rank the distances and identify the K = 3 nearest neighbors. Make sure to show your intermediate calculations.

Based on the data listed in the table below, classify the new call as an Alarm call or a Contact call. Use a K-NN classification with K = 3. Provide the probability that the new call is an Alarm call.
cases.symbols: \(x_i\) (feature vector of training entry \(i\)), \(y_i\) (its class label), \(L\) (number of classes), \(K\) (number of nearest neighbors), \(d\) (Euclidean distance).

steps.title: Set up
steps.words: The training set has five labeled calls.

steps.title: Distances
steps.words: Compute the distance from the new call to every labeled call.

steps.title: Rank the distances
steps.words: Ranks are B 1, C 2, E 3, D 4, A 5, so the K = 3 nearest neighbors are B, C and E.

steps.title: Read the neighbor classes
steps.words: The other labeled calls are not neighbors, so their classes are not used.

steps.title: Classify and give the probability
steps.words: Alarm is the plurality class, so the new call is classified as an Alarm call.

cases.conclusion: The three nearest neighbors are B (Alarm), C (Contact) and E (Alarm). The new call is classified as an Alarm call, with probability 2/3 of being an Alarm call.

cases.title: Classifying a brain scan as patient or control with K = 3
cases.context: In a brain imaging study of memory decline, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans of 6 adults were used to measure hippocampal volume (the volume of a brain structure needed to form new memories, in mm³) and cortical thickness (the thickness of the outer layer of the brain, in mm). Three scans came from patients with a diagnosed memory disorder (Patient) and three came from healthy adults of the same age (Control). The data were standardized to avoid any issues associated with differences in scale; the scaled data are unitless. A new scan had a scaled hippocampal volume of 4 and a scaled cortical thickness of 4. The 6 labeled scans were measured with the following results (training set):
tasks: Calculate the Euclidean distance from the new scan (4, 4) to each of the 6 labeled scans, rank the distances and identify the K = 3 nearest neighbors. Make sure to show your intermediate calculations.
Based on the data listed in the table below, classify the new scan as Patient or Control. Use a K-NN classification with K = 3. Provide the probability that the new scan is from a patient.
cases.symbols: \(x_i\) (feature vector of training entry \(i\)), \(y_i\) (its class label), \(L\) (number of classes), \(K\) (number of nearest neighbors), \(d\) (Euclidean distance).

steps.title: Set up
steps.words: The training set has six labeled scans.

steps.title: Distances
steps.words: Compute the distance from the new scan to every labeled scan.

steps.title: Rank the distances
steps.words: Ranks are D 1, A 2, B 3, C 4, F 5, E 6, so the K = 3 nearest neighbors are D, A and B.

steps.words: The other labeled scans are not neighbors, so their classes are not used.

questions.stem: Researchers recorded the average bedtime and the average wake time of 200 students with wrist activity monitors. No student had been given a chronotype label. The researchers wanted to find out whether the students fall into natural groups. Which task is this?
options: Classification, because the groups will be given names afterwards
Clustering, because only the features \(x_i\) are given and no labels \(y_i\) exist
Classification, because there are two features
Regression, because bedtime is a continuous measure
questions.why: No labels are known in advance, so the task is clustering (unsupervised). Classification needs a training set with known labels \(y_i\).

questions.stem: Student A has (extraversion, neuroticism) scores of (14, 32) points and student B has (28, 23) points. What is the Euclidean distance between the two score profiles?
questions.why: The differences are 14 and 9, so \(\sqrt{196+81}=\sqrt{277}\approx 16.64332\). 277 forgets the square root, 23 is the Manhattan distance and 5 subtracts the two differences.

questions.stem: Patient 1 has (anxiety, low mood) scores of (17, 9) points and patient 2 has (11, 20) points. What is the Minkowski distance with \(p=3\) between the two symptom profiles?
questions.why: Cube the absolute differences 6 and 11, add, and take the cube root. \(1547^{1/3}\approx 11.56547\). 1547 skips the root, 515.66667 divides by 3 instead of taking a root, and 12.52996 is the Euclidean distance.

questions.stem: Nine average bedtimes (15, 30, 40, 85, 120, 150, 165, 180 and 195 min after 9 pm) are clustered with \(k=2\), \(c_1=30\) and \(c_2=100\). After iteration 1, what is the new centroid of cluster 2?
questions.why: In iteration 1 cluster 2 holds 85, 120, 150, 165, 180 and 195, so \(895/6\approx 149.16667\). 162 is the iteration 2 centroid, 179 divides by 5 instead of 6, and 100 is the old centroid.

questions.stem: Four mice have scaled (Centre time, Distance) values of (1, 2), (3, 2), (6, 5) and (7, 8). After a single k-Means iteration with initial centroids C1 = (1, 1) and C2 = (5, 5), what is the new centroid C2?
questions.why: Mice 3 and 4 are closer to C2, so the new C2 is the mean of (6, 5) and (7, 8), which is (6.5, 6.5). (5, 5) is the old centroid, (4.25, 4.25) averages all four mice, and (13, 13) adds without dividing by 2.

questions.stem: Reaction time (about 200 to 700 ms) and error rate (about 0.01 to 0.20) were measured in 30 children and are to be clustered with the k-Means algorithm and the Euclidean distance. Why are the two measures standardized first?
options: Otherwise reaction time, which has much larger numbers, would decide almost all of the distance
Standardizing gives every child a cluster label before the algorithm starts
The Euclidean distance cannot be calculated for values that have units
Standardizing fixes the number of clusters at k = 2
questions.why: The Euclidean distance adds squared differences across features, so a feature with a large numeric range dominates. Standardizing puts both features on a comparable, unitless scale.

questions.stem: Ten hearing thresholds are clustered by R into 6, 9, 12, 15, 21 (centroid 12.6) and 48, 52, 57, 63, 68 (centroid 57.6). The total sum of squares is 5456.9. What is tot.withinss for \(k=2\)?
questions.why: The two within-cluster sums of squares are 133.2 and 261.2, and they add to 394.4. 5062.5 is betweenss, 133.2 is cluster 1 alone and 5456.9 is the total sum of squares.

questions.stem: Symptom scores of 60 patients are clustered with kmeans() in R for \(k=1\) to 6, and tot.withinss gets smaller at every step. How should the number of clusters be chosen?
options: Choose the k with the smallest tot.withinss, which is k = 6
Choose the k with the largest tot.withinss, which is k = 1
Choose the k where betweenss equals tot.withinss
Choose the k after which tot.withinss improves only modestly
questions.why: tot.withinss always falls as k grows and reaches 0 when every entry is its own cluster, so the smallest value is not a useful rule. The chosen k is the one beyond which further gains are modest.

questions.stem: A new songbird call at (5, 5) is compared with the labeled calls A (2, 7) Alarm, B (3, 5) Alarm, C (6, 3) Contact, D (8, 6) Contact and E (5, 8) Alarm. With K-NN and \(K=3\), what is the probability that the new call is an Alarm call?
questions.why: The three nearest calls are B (2), C (2.23607) and E (3). Two of the three are Alarm calls, so the probability is 2/3. 0.6 uses all five calls, 0.33333 is the Contact probability and 1 uses only the single nearest call.

questions.stem: A new brain scan is classified with K-NN and \(K=3\). Its closest labeled scan is a control, and the second and third closest labeled scans are patients. How is the new scan classified?
options: Control, because the single closest scan decides the class
It cannot be classified, because the neighbors disagree
Patient, because the plurality class among the K = 3 nearest scans decides
Control, because closer neighbors always get more votes
questions.why: K-NN counts the classes of the K nearest neighbors and assigns the most common one. Two of the three neighbors are patients, so the scan is classified as a patient with probability 2/3.

notes: All data are invented for practice. Every lookup is null because no printed critical value is used in this session.

The exercise wording is kept with its own punctuation in context and tasks (the semicolon in "differences in scale; the scaled data are unitless", the colon after "initial centroids" and after "(training set)"). The check script allows colons and semicolons in context and tasks only. Abbreviations in parentheses use commas.

The 1-D k-means case and both withinss cases store the raw data under the values key "ages" because the reference cases of those methods use that key name. The data are bedtimes (min after 9 pm), hearing thresholds (dB HL) and cortisol (nmol/L).

The withinss tables were produced with R's kmeans(). k = 2 used the starting centres named in the context. k = 3 and k = 4 used set.seed(1) and nstart = 50, and the cluster order and number formatting are as R printed them. The check script confirms that the k = 3 and k = 4 totals are the global minimum over all partitions.
n22-b-cortisol-withinss is built so that the elbow is at k = 3, not k = 2. The hand calculation is still done for the k = 2 output, as in the reference case.
n22-b-brain-scan-knn is built so that the single nearest scan is a control but K = 3 classifies the scan as a patient.
Both 2-D k-means cases are a single iteration, as in the reference exercise case. No distance ties occur in any case.

n22-b-cortisol-withinss: the starting centres in the context are c(8, 29). Started from 8 and 29 the hand algorithm reaches the reported 7 / 3 split in one step with no tie. The earlier c(6, 25) hit an exact tie (17 is 7.4 from both centroids) and ended 5 / 5. No table value or answer changed.
